items.stem: State what is meant by the term "comparative essay".
items.answer: An essay that identifies and explains both similarities (comparisons) and differences (contrasts) between two examples, such as two wars or two leaders
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an essay that identifies and explains both similarities (comparisons) and differences (contrasts) between two examples, such as two wars or two leaders. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A student claims that comparative essays only need to discuss similarities. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Compare-and-contrast questions require both similarities and differences; a response with only one cannot reach the top bands.
items.markingKey: Compare-and-contrast questions require both similarities and differences; a response with only one cannot reach the top bands. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that a Paper 2 essay is best written by describing everything known about two wars. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Examiners reward focused analysis that answers the question; irrelevant detail and narrative limit the mark.
items.markingKey: Examiners reward focused analysis that answers the question; irrelevant detail and narrative limit the mark. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Nia writes: "A Paper 2 essay is best written by describing everything known about two wars." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Examiners reward focused analysis that answers the question; irrelevant detail and narrative limit the mark.
items.markingKey: Examiners reward focused analysis that answers the question; irrelevant detail and narrative limit the mark. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source B
Without the German and Italian transport aircraft that ferried the Army of Africa across the Strait of Gibraltar in the summer of 1936, the military rising might well have failed in its first weeks. Foreign help did not merely sustain Franco; it rescued him at the outset.
— Antony Beevor, British historian, The Battle for Spain: The Spanish Civil War 1936–1939 (2006) (paraphrased)

Identify three points made in Source B about foreign intervention in the Spanish and Chinese civil wars. [3]
items.answer: German and Italian aircraft airlifted the Army of Africa in 1936; without them the rising might have failed early; foreign help rescued Franco at the start, not just later.
items.markingKey: German and Italian aircraft airlifted the Army of Africa in 1936; without them the rising might have failed early; foreign help rescued Franco at the start, not just later. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must be taken from the source; own knowledge is not credited in Question 1.

items.stem: Outline one way in which a plan for “Evaluate the impact of the Cold War on two countries, each from a different region” shows selecting examples to fit the demands of the question.
items.answer: A strong plan selects Cuba (Americas) and Korea (Asia), considering political, economic and social impact. Choosing contrasting countries from different regions satisfies the question’s requirements and allows evaluation.
items.markingKey: Context (A strong plan selects Cuba (Americas) and Korea (Asia), considering political, economic and social impact.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Choosing contrasting countries from different regions satisfies the question’s requirements and allows evaluation. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to selecting examples to fit the demands of the question.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the Chinese Civil War and the Spanish Civil War were won by the side that received most foreign support.
items.answer: Foreign support was decisive in Spain but not in China, where internal factors were more important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Franco’s German and Italian aid; Soviet help to the CCP in Manchuria in 1945–46. Arguments against: US aid to the GMD exceeded Soviet aid to the CCP; CCP victory owed most to peasant mobilisation; Republican divisions in Spain. Supported judgement: Foreign support was decisive in Spain but not in China, where internal factors were more important.

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source B, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating foreign intervention in the Spanish and Chinese civil wars. [4]
items.answer: Value: Beevor is a respected military historian who drew on Spanish, German and Soviet archives, giving a well-evidenced judgement on the importance of the airlift. Limitations: As a narrative military history it focuses on operations; the counterfactual claim that the rising “might well have failed” cannot be proved and may underplay Nationalist strengths.

items.stem: Explain why choosing appropriate examples is important in Paper 2.
items.answer: Examples must fit the question (e.g. two wars from different regions for a causes question); well-chosen, contrasting examples such as the Spanish Civil War and the Chinese Civil War allow detailed comparison and support analysis.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Examples must fit the question (e.g. two wars from different regions for a causes question); well-chosen, contrasting examples such as the Spanish Civil War and the Chinese Civil War allow detailed comparison and support analysis. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which a plan for “Compare and contrast the causes of two civil wars, each from a different region” shows thematic comparison in Paper 2.
items.answer: A strong plan uses the Spanish Civil War (Europe) and the Chinese Civil War (Asia), with paragraphs on ideological, economic and political causes and the role of foreign intervention. Each paragraph compares both wars on one cause, making similarities and differences explicit and supporting a judgement.
items.markingKey: Context (A strong plan uses the Spanish Civil War (Europe) and the Chinese Civil War (Asia), with paragraphs on ideological, economic and political causes and the role of foreign intervention.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Each paragraph compares both wars on one cause, making similarities and differences explicit and supporting a judgement. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to thematic comparison in Paper 2.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Detailed, precise and accurate knowledge of a region, including names, dates, statistics and developments, used to support analysis"?
items.answer: depth of knowledge
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of depth of knowledge.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Paper 2 and Paper 3.
items.answer: Paper 2 requires two essays on world history topics, often comparative across regions; Paper 3 (HL only) requires three essays on a single region in greater depth.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 requires two essays on world history topics, often comparative across regions; Paper 3 (HL only) requires three essays on a single region in greater depth. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "In Paper 3 the more facts included, the higher the mark." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Knowledge is rewarded only when relevant and used to support analysis; a list of facts without argument stays in the middle bands.
items.markingKey: Knowledge is rewarded only when relevant and used to support analysis; a list of facts without argument stays in the middle bands. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source B
The Great Leap Forward was not simply a failed economic policy. It was a catastrophe in which coercion, terror and systematic violence were the foundation of the system, and in which perhaps 45 million people died unnecessarily.
— Frank Dikötter, historian, Mao’s Great Famine (2010) (paraphrased)

What is the message conveyed by Source B? [2]
items.answer: The Great Leap was a catastrophe rather than merely a failed policy; violence and coercion were central; around 45 million died unnecessarily.

items.stem:
Source A
The famine was caused by policy mistakes that were compounded by the political system. Local officials, fearful after the Lushan Conference, competed to report higher outputs, and the centre took the figures at face value.
— Yang Jisheng, Chinese journalist and historian, Tombstone (2008) (paraphrased)

What, according to Source A, were the main features of the Great Leap Forward and the famine of 1959–1961? [3]
items.answer: The famine resulted from policy mistakes worsened by the political system; officials feared punishment after Lushan; false reports were accepted by the centre.
items.markingKey: The famine resulted from policy mistakes worsened by the political system; officials feared punishment after Lushan; false reports were accepted by the centre. items.stem: To what extent did the Cultural Revolution achieve Mao’s aims? [15]
items.answer: Mao achieved his short-term political aims, but the long-term ideological goals failed.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: removal of rivals (Liu Shaoqi, Deng); mobilisation of youth; chaos and economic disruption; reversal after 1976. items.stem: Distinguish between evaluating historians’ interpretations and using historians as evidence.
items.answer: Using historians as evidence cites their conclusions to support a point; evaluating interpretations assesses why historians differ and how convincing their arguments are.

items.answer: Interpretations show awareness of different perspectives and that history is debated; evaluating them (their evidence and context) supports the candidate’s own judgement – a top-band descriptor. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

items.stem: Using debates on Partition (Jalal and others) as an example, explain revisionist interpretations in regional history.
items.answer: Ayesha Jalal’s The Sole Spokesman (1985) challenged the view that Jinnah always sought a separate Pakistan. New interpretations can reshape understanding of key figures and encourage evaluation of earlier views.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against the view that historians’ interpretations of the origins of the Second World War have been shaped more by the evidence available than by the times in which they wrote.
items.answer: Evidence and context both shape interpretation; their influence varies by historian and period.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: captured German documents and Nuremberg evidence shaped early views; Soviet archives after 1991; Hossbach debate turned on documents. Arguments against: Taylor reacting against the “guilty men” orthodoxy; Cold War context of early works; appeasement debates linked to contemporary policy (Suez, Iraq). Supported judgement: Evidence and context both shape interpretation; their influence varies by historian and period.

An historian’s explanation or judgement about the past, based on evidence and shaped by questions, sources and context
The order of events; a clear grasp of chronology allows analysis of causation and change over time
The study of how history has been written and of how and why interpretations of the past differ and change

Source D
The Soviet system could have survived for years longer through repression and the use of force. That it did not was above all the result of the choices made by Gorbachev, who decided that the Soviet Union would no longer hold Eastern Europe by tanks.
— Archie Brown, British political scientist, The Gorbachev Factor (1996) (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source D, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the end of the Cold War. [4]
items.answer: Value: Brown is a leading specialist on Soviet politics who interviewed many Soviet officials, giving an informed view of Gorbachev’s role. Limitations: Written soon after the events and focused on one leader, it may overstate individual agency and underplay economic decline and popular movements.

items.stem: Evaluate the validity of the view that the Great Leap Forward was the greatest failure of Mao’s rule. [15]
items.answer: The Great Leap was Mao’s greatest failure in human terms, though the Cultural Revolution did more long-term political damage.
items.markingKey: Paper 3 essay. Indicative content: famine of 30–45 million deaths; industrial and agricultural collapse; loss of Soviet support; the Cultural Revolution’s social and cultural destruction; Anti-Rightist Campaign; some infrastructure gains. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: The Great Leap was Mao’s greatest failure in human terms, though the Cultural Revolution did more long-term political damage. Markbands – 13–15: clearly focused and well structured; in-depth, accurate and relevant knowledge used effectively to support analysis; examples are appropriate and comparisons/contrasts are developed where relevant; evaluation of different perspectives integrated into the argument; reasoned conclusion consistent with the evidence; 10–12: demands clearly understood; clearly structured with effective focus; accurate and relevant knowledge; events placed in context and some understanding of historical concepts; critical analysis with main points substantiated; some evaluation of different perspectives; consistent conclusion; 7–9: demands understood but not all implications considered; some clear structure; mostly accurate and relevant knowledge, with events placed in context; some critical analysis, though it may be partly narrative; some awareness of different perspectives; 4–6: some indication of the demands; some structure; some knowledge but lacking accuracy or relevance; mostly narrative or descriptive; limited analysis; 1–3: little understanding of the demands of the question; poorly structured or no clear structure; little relevant knowledge; no analysis or evaluation; 0: does not reach a standard described by the descriptors below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that historians’ interpretations of the origins of the Second World War have been shaped more by the evidence available than by the times in which they wrote.
items.answer: Evidence and context both shape interpretation; their influence varies by historian and period.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: captured German documents and Nuremberg evidence shaped early views; Soviet archives after 1991; Hossbach debate turned on documents. Arguments against: Taylor reacting against the “guilty men” orthodoxy; Cold War context of early works; appeasement debates linked to contemporary policy (Suez, Iraq). Supported judgement: Evidence and context both shape interpretation; their influence varies by historian and period. Markbands (10 marks): Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, in-depth accurate knowledge supporting critical analysis, perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – limited understanding of the demands, mainly description.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An essay organisation in which each paragraph addresses one theme or factor across both examples, rather than dealing with each example in turn"?
items.answer: thematic structure
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of thematic structure.

items.stem: How many essays must candidates answer in Paper 3?
items.answer: Three
items.markingKey: A. Each essay is marked out of 15, giving a total of 45 marks.

items.stem: Briefly explain why using historians’ interpretations can strengthen an essay.
items.answer: Interpretations show awareness of different perspectives and that history is debated; evaluating them (their evidence and context) supports the candidate’s own judgement – a top-band descriptor.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Interpretations show awareness of different perspectives and that history is debated; evaluating them (their evidence and context) supports the candidate’s own judgement – a top-band descriptor. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between an essay in the 7–9 markband and an essay in the 13–15 markband.
items.answer: A 7–9 essay understands the demands of the question and shows mostly accurate knowledge but is partly narrative; a 13–15 essay is clearly focused and well structured, uses in-depth knowledge to support critical analysis, evaluates perspectives and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: A 7–9 essay understands the demands of the question and shows mostly accurate knowledge but is partly narrative; a 13–15 essay is clearly focused and well structured, uses in-depth knowledge to support critical analysis, evaluates perspectives and reaches a reasoned conclusion. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a narrative essay and a comparative essay.
items.answer: A comparative essay analyses similarities and differences in relation to the question; a narrative essay tells the story of events and rarely earns marks above the middle bands.
items.markingKey: A comparative essay analyses similarities and differences in relation to the question; a narrative essay tells the story of events and rarely earns marks above the middle bands. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why candidates should avoid narrative in Paper 3 essays.
items.answer: Narrative tells what happened without explaining why or how far; the markbands reward critical analysis, so knowledge must be used as evidence for an argument.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Narrative tells what happened without explaining why or how far; the markbands reward critical analysis, so knowledge must be used as evidence for an argument. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Kenji writes: "A later interpretation is always more accurate than an earlier one." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Later historians may have more evidence, but interpretations reflect their questions and context; a later view is not automatically correct.
items.markingKey: Later historians may have more evidence, but interpretations reflect their questions and context; a later view is not automatically correct. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using self-assessment of a Paper 3 essay on Partition as an example, explain using markbands to improve essays.
items.answer: The student’s essay narrated events from 1940 to 1947 with few judgements; comparing it with the markbands placed it in the 7–9 band. The student identified the need to turn narrative into analysis and to evaluate interpretations.
items.markingKey: Context (The student’s essay narrated events from 1940 to 1947 with few judgements; comparing it with the markbands placed it in the 7–9 band.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The student identified the need to turn narrative into analysis and to evaluate interpretations. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using markbands to improve essays.

items.stem:
Source C
Without the German and Italian transport aircraft that ferried the Army of Africa across the Strait of Gibraltar in the summer of 1936, the military rising might well have failed in its first weeks. Foreign help did not merely sustain Franco; it rescued him at the outset.
— Antony Beevor, British historian, The Battle for Spain: The Spanish Civil War 1936–1939 (2006) (paraphrased)

Outline the message that the author of Source C intended to convey. [2]
items.answer: German and Italian aircraft airlifted the Army of Africa in 1936; without them the rising might have failed early; foreign help rescued Franco at the start, not just later.
items.markingKey: German and Italian aircraft airlifted the Army of Africa in 1936; without them the rising might have failed early; foreign help rescued Franco at the start, not just later. Award 1 mark for each valid point about the message, up to [2]; a description of the source without interpretation of its message scores at most 1.

items.stem:
Source A
The Great Leap Forward was not simply a failed economic policy. It was a catastrophe in which coercion, terror and systematic violence were the foundation of the system, and in which perhaps 45 million people died unnecessarily.
— Frank Dikötter, historian, Mao’s Great Famine (2010) (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source A, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating the Great Leap Forward and the famine of 1959–1961. [4]
items.answer: Value: Dikötter used provincial party archives that had recently become accessible, giving detailed evidence. Limitations: His estimate is at the high end of scholarly figures, and some historians argue he emphasises violence over policy errors.
items.markingKey: Value: Dikötter used provincial party archives that had recently become accessible, giving detailed evidence. Limitations: His estimate is at the high end of scholarly figures, and some historians argue he emphasises violence over policy errors. Award up to [4]: origin, purpose and content must each be referred to and linked to value or limitation for the stated enquiry. If only values or only limitations are discussed, award a maximum of [2]. Listing provenance without explaining its effect on value is not rewarded.

items.stem:
Source B
It is the function of the historian to interpret the past, and therefore historians will always disagree. Each generation rewrites history in the light of its own concerns.
— Summary of a common historiographical argument, based on Pieter Geyl, Napoleon: For and Against (1949) (paraphrased)

What is the message conveyed by Source B? [2]
items.answer: Historians interpret the past and will always disagree; each generation rewrites history according to its concerns.
items.markingKey: Historians interpret the past and will always disagree; each generation rewrites history according to its concerns. Award 1 mark for each valid point about the message, up to [2]; a description of the source without interpretation of its message scores at most 1.

items.stem: Briefly describe a timed essay on “Examine the reasons for the outbreak of the Korean War” and explain what it reveals about effective time management in essays.
items.answer: A student spends five minutes planning causes (Kim’s ambitions, Stalin’s approval, Acheson speech, civil conflict), writes for 40 minutes and checks the conclusion. A clear plan allows focus on the question within the time limit and prevents narrative.
items.markingKey: Context (A student spends five minutes planning causes (Kim’s ambitions, Stalin’s approval, Acheson speech, civil conflict), writes for 40 minutes and checks the conclusion.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A clear plan allows focus on the question within the time limit and prevents narrative. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to effective time management in essays.

items.stem:
Source B
Soviet help in Manchuria in 1945–46, above all the handover of captured Japanese weapons, gave the communists a secure base. But the outcome of the war was decided by the Guomindang’s strategic blunders and its failure to keep the confidence of the cities, not by Moscow, whose aid remained cautious.
— Odd Arne Westad, historian, Decisive Encounters: The Chinese Civil War, 1946–1950 (2003) (paraphrased)

With reference to the origin, purpose and content of Source B, assess its values and limitations for historians investigating foreign intervention in the Spanish and Chinese civil wars. [4]
items.answer: Value: Westad is a leading historian of the Cold War in Asia who used Chinese and Russian archives, so he can weigh foreign and domestic factors. Limitations: His focus on the 1946–50 period gives less weight to longer-term factors such as the Japanese war and CCP rural mobilisation in Yan’an.

items.stem: Evaluate the contribution of historiographical debate to our understanding of the causes of the Cold War. [15]
items.answer: Historiographical debate has enriched understanding by broadening the questions and evidence considered.
items.markingKey: Paper 2 essay. Indicative content: orthodox, revisionist and post-revisionist schools; impact of new archives; non-superpower perspectives (Westad); limits of debate focused on blame. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Historiographical debate has enriched understanding by broadening the questions and evidence considered.
